sum: In compliance with paragraphs 6.77 to 6.89 of the Listings Requirements of the JSE Limited (“the JSE Listings Requirements”), shareholders are advised of the following transaction. Remgro chair Rupert warns uncertain global landscape no longer episodic
sum: Remgro chair Johann Rupert has warned investors that uncertainty will no longer be episodic but will remain a defining feature of the global landscape.

Writing in the group’s latest annual report, Rupert highlighted that slower global growth, geopolitical tension, inflation risk, elevated sovereign debt levels and capital market volatility all have the potential to affect investing outcomes.
He added that increasing political polarisation and protectionist policy tendencies are additional concerns.
“Political developments in major economies and in South Africa will continue to influence confidence and provide indicators for policy direction in an increasingly complex world economy,” he said.

Rupert said the global environment in the past year had been volatile and uncertain characterised by geopolitical tension, armed conflict, persistent fiscal pressure in many major economies, shifting trade patterns, rapid technological change and the advance of artificial intelligence. It continued to reshape the way capital, labour and ideas move across borders.

“These forces are not only creating new efficiencies and opportunities, but they also require careful judgment, particularly where technological progress raises questions of trust, social cohesion and the responsible use of innovation.”

In South Africa, the operating environment remained difficult, though not without signs of progress, he said. He cited lower inflation, a more stable energy environment, and greater collaboration between the public and private sectors as encouraging signs.

South Africa’s $30 billion succession: what the Rupert, Oppenheimer and le Roux heirs inherit
sum: The three men behind South Africa’s largest private fortunes are 76, 77 and 81. Their sons stand to inherit very different things, and only one of them is being groomed in public.

South Africa’s three largest fortunes belong to men born before 1951. Johann Rupert, chairman of Swiss luxury group Richemont, is 76 and worth roughly $15 billion on recent market estimates. Nicky Oppenheimer, 81, whose family controlled De Beers for more than 80 years, holds about $10.8 billion. Michiel le Roux, 77, co-founder of Capitec, has about $3.8 billion. Together they account for close to $30 billion, a sum that moves with the share prices of a Geneva-based luxury group and a Stellenbosch bank.

Each man has a son in line. The resemblance ends there. Anton Rupert, 39, is being placed inside the governance of a listed company his family controls with a minority of its equity. Jonathan Oppenheimer, 56, already runs a family office whose wealth was converted to cash 14 years ago. The younger Michiel le Roux built his own lender elsewhere in Africa and has no role at Capitec. For investors in Richemont, Remgro and Capitec, those differences decide how much a change of generation will be felt in the boardroom and on the share register.

On September 9, Richemont named Anton Rupert non-executive co-deputy chairman, with immediate effect. He shares the title with Bram Schot, 65, the former Audi chief executive who joined the board in 2023 and became deputy chairman in 2024. The board split the job. Schot handles governance and the coordination of board committees; Rupert oversees the Strategic Product and Communications Committee, which sets product and messaging priorities across Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and the group’s other maisons. Johann Rupert called the appointment “an important step in the Board’s long-term succession planning.”

The younger Rupert has sat on Richemont’s board since 2017 and has also served as a director of Remgro. He keeps a low public profile. His best-known roles have been at family concerns such as L’Ormarins, the Rupert wine estate in Franschhoek, and the Franschhoek Motor Museum.
Outside shareholders should care because of the share structure.

Optasia EBITDA rises 45% with further optimistic prospects in sight
sum: Optasia reported strong growth in the first half of 2026, with revenue rising 58% to $185.3 million and adjusted EBITDA increasing 45% to $77.9m.
The financial-intelligence and technology-enabled credit-solutions group reported its first set of results since listing on the JSE in November.
Normalised net income increased 40% to $39.3m, while adjusted free cash flow rose 150% to $32.7m.

Chief executive officer Salvador Anglada said in an online presentation that the group had delivered growth “across all parameters”. He attributed the performance partly to Optasia’s diversification across 35 countries.
Anglada said the group had continued to expand despite weaker growth in Nigeria, where airtime-credit services were temporarily suspended by regulators through April
Microfinance solutions, or MFS, remained the group’s main growth driver. Revenue from the division increased 84% and accounted for 72% of group revenue, compared with 62% in the first half of 2025.
Ghana continued to scale strongly, while Pakistan, Indonesia and the Republic of the Congo also delivered strong results, the company said.
